docs.title: PEAT
docs.text:
Protein Engineering Agent Toolkit

PEAT is a chat interface for protein redesign. You state a design goal in prose — "redesign 1UBQ to improve thermostability" — and a LangGraph agent loads the reference structure, proposes variants, folds and scores them, ranks an ensemble and writes the round up as an artifact you can read, download or keep working from. The slow work does not run on the web server: it is pushed to your HPC allocation through your endpoint, and the model calls go to your LLM key.

docs.title: What it is for
docs.text:
The whole design follows from one constraint: a chat interface must answer in milliseconds, while a fold takes tens of seconds and a cluster job takes hours. Every unit of work is therefore submitted asynchronously and returns a handle immediately; the conversation continues while the jobs run, and the reply names what is still in flight.

A session looks like this. You name a target, and the agent retrieves its structure from the RCSB PDB or the AlphaFold database, its annotation from UniProt and the relevant literature from Europe PMC. You give it a goal, and it picks a success metric, dispatches a round of design work — ProteinMPNN on the cluster where an endpoint is attached, a labelled heuristic proposer where one is not — folds and scores what comes back, ranks an ensemble, and loops until the metric stops improving. Then it summarizes, renders a Markdown and .docx report and an interactive Mol* view, and files every design, task and output in a tiered data lake.

What you supply is an Anthropic API key and, for real compute, a RADICAL Orbit broker, endpoint, account and queue. What persists is the lake: a later session, yours or a colleague's on the same deployment, reads back the best designs from earlier campaigns and says so in its summary.

For a longer multi-day campaign there is a second mode. The protocol node runs an enzyme-redesign pipeline — conservation analysis, ProteinMPNN redesign, selection, AlphaFold3 folding, report — as one cluster stage per chat turn, using the turn boundary itself as the place a run stops and waits for a human decision.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Interactive design rounds. A conversation, not a submit script: state a goal, watch the tasks, read the round, ask for another.
  • Bring your own LLM and HPC. Each signed-in user supplies their own Anthropic key and their own Orbit broker, endpoint, account and queue; a turn runs under the credentials of the person who asked.
  • Three task interfaces. local for CPU work in a process pool, query for REST retrieval on the event loop, hpc for real scheduler jobs — same submit-and-handle contract for all three.
  • A design history that outlives the session. A three-tier lake — provenance graph, scores, curated Parquet sets — that later campaigns read back from.
  • A multi-day protocol, one stage per turn. Nine stages with human checkpoints where the science needs one.
  • Honest degradation. With no API key every node falls back to a deterministic rule-based path; with no endpoint, ProteinMPNN falls back to a heuristic proposer that says so in the output rather than passing itself off as a model run. Every user-visible sentence carries the name of the function that wrote it.

docs.title: What runs today
docs.text:
Read this before cloning

  • A fresh clone cannot be built. The four middleware packages are local editable installs from a refcodes/ directory that is gitignored, so ./scripts/setup.sh on a clean clone stops and tells you what is missing. See Installation and plans/BACKLOG.md (A fresh clone cannot be built).
  • No stage of the enzyme-redesign protocol has yet run on a cluster, so every walltime, core count and memory figure in protocol/specs.py is an estimate. The hpc path itself has run for real — submit, poll, tail, cancel, with the Slurm job id coming back.
  • The Globus Compute adapter has never met a live endpoint. It implements the same interface and is tested offline; that is all.
  • The Python package and the environment prefix are still designagent and DESIGNAGENT_. Nothing here imports as peat.
  • This is a from-scratch rewrite that shares no history with the Streamlit application that previously carried the name; that work is preserved on the repository's archive/* branches.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
PEAT is four cooperating pieces: a web frontend that streams a conversation and renders what it produces, an agentic app that decides what to do and writes every user-visible sentence, a task interface layer that gets slow work off the event loop and onto the right substrate, and a data lake that remembers what happened after the session ends.

They exist in that shape because of one constraint — a chat must answer in milliseconds, a fold takes tens of seconds, and a cluster job takes hours. Everything below is downstream of it.

flowchart LR
  B["browser"] <-->|SSE| A["app.py<br/>FastAPI"]
  A --> G["LangGraph loop<br/>6 nodes"]
  G -->|Deps| T["TaskManager"]
  T --> L["local"]
  T --> Q["query"]
  T --> H["hpc"]
  G --> D["DesignHistory<br/>Kuzu · SQLite · Parquet"]

docs.title: The web frontend
docs.text:
frontend/ is a React 19 application built by Vite 6, with four runtime dependencies in total: react, react-dom, marked and dompurify. It is split into two panes.

The chat pane holds the conversation, the live status lines a turn emits, and a task chip per unit of work. A chip names its interface whenever that interface is not local, so a ProteinMPNN task reads hpc, and expanding it shows a streaming log tail — which only the Orbit/PSI-J path can produce, because log streaming is a declared capability the local interfaces do not have. Under each reply there is a how this answer was made disclosure: the node that produced the text, the function inside it, and the per-node timings of the turn.

The artifact pane renders what a round produces: an interactive structure view, the session summary as Markdown, the ensemble table, and a downloadable .docx. The viewer is Mol* — specifically @rcsb/rcsb-molstar, which is not an npm dependency: frontend/src/artifacts/MolstarView.tsx loads a pinned UMD build from a CDN at runtime and caches the loader on window.

Two deliberate restrictions are worth knowing. Assistant text is model-influenced, so it is sanitized before it is rendered. And the visualization the agent produces is a JSON view spec that the frontend validates field by field, never generated JavaScript — shipping model-written JS into the page would let a prompt put code in the browser, so a bad generation degrades to a plain cartoon instead.

docs.title: The agentic app
docs.text:
backend/designagent/app.py is a FastAPI service: login and session routes, a Server-Sent-Events chat endpoint, artifact and task routes, settings, and a health endpoint that reports which degraded modes are in effect. Behind it is a LangGraph loop of six nodes.

Node Does Writes to state Coordinator Classifies the prompt, streams updates, answers from state intent, goal Design Initializer PDB, UniProt and literature lookups, concurrently reference_design Redesign Orchestrator Picks the success metric, builds and dispatches the worklist key_metric, worklist Analyst Scores returns, writes the lake, ranks, rebuilds the view lead_design, ensemble, molecular_visualization Interpreter Summarizes, flags related past designs, renders artifacts design_summary, artifacts Protocol Runs one stage of the enzyme-redesign cluster pipeline per turn protocol

Five rules describe the loop more usefully than a call graph:

  • Routing is dynamic. A node returns Command(goto=..., update=...), so the routing decision and the state write are one atomic return; START → coordinator is the only static edge. A chat turn ends immediately, a design request loops Orchestrator → Analyst until the key metric stops improving or max_rounds is reached, then summarizes.
  • Nodes reach the outside only through Deps. Settings, the task manager, the design history and the artifact store are injected (graph/deps.py); no node imports a store or an interface. This is the reason the 417-test offline suite needs no network, no process pool and no endpoint.
  • State carries no bulky payloads. LangGraph serializes a checkpoint every turn, so coordinates go to a content-addressed blob and travel as a path. A test asserts that ATOM records never appear in serialized state, because the regression is otherwise invisible — nothing breaks, the checkpoint just grows every turn.
  • Only prose streams to the chat. Streaming is opt-in per call, and only the two user-facing calls use it; the intent classifier's and round planner's JSON are explicitly suppressed, or they would arrive in the assistant's bubble.
  • Every user-visible sentence is attributable. A node that authors text records a reply_source such as interpreter:_rule_based_summary or coordinator:llm — a value that greps straight to the function that wrote it. Without this, a reply reads identically whether a rule or a model produced it.

With no API key the loop still runs end to end: every node has a deterministic rule-based path, and the key improves classification, planning and the written summary rather than enabling them. When a key is present but rejected, the turn says so in its own reply instead of looking normal.

docs.title: The protocol node
docs.text:
The other five nodes serve a chat turn. graph/nodes/protocol.py serves a multi-day cluster pipeline — the enzyme-redesign protocol — as one stage per turn: nine stages from intake through conservation analysis, ProteinMPNN redesign, selection and AlphaFold3 to the report. It is the only node that answers the user every turn and never routes onward.

The protocol has points where a run must stop and wait for a person, and there is no interrupt() anywhere in this codebase. The turn boundary is the checkpoint mechanism: a stage sets an awaiting key and returns, and the next message answers it. That has one visible consequence — while a campaign is waiting, the coordinator routes to the protocol node before it classifies intent at all, because answers like "liu", "310,364" and "go" would otherwise classify as chat and leave the campaign waiting forever. A short list of escape words is the way out.

Progress is read from the filesystem, never from a task handle. Handles are in-memory, so a restarted server cannot re-attach to an in-flight job; the collect stage lists the output tree and reads the small summary files instead, which makes it idempotent and identical whether the submission was minutes or days ago. The data outlives the handle, so recovery is a re-fetch, not a re-attach.

Everything a chat message contributes — a target name, a UniProt id, domain bounds, catalytic residues, a cluster account name — ends up inside a bash -lc body and in paths the endpoint writes to under the site's allocation. The input validators therefore reject rather than sanitize, and the protocol's own settings are environment-only, never writable over HTTP, for the same reason.

docs.title: The task interfaces
docs.text:
Task duration is indeterminate, so every interface submits asynchronously and returns a handle carrying a future. Nothing in the graph awaits at submission time, and a failed submission becomes a settled FAILED handle rather than an exception — so callers have exactly one shape to handle and gathering results never raises.

Interface Backing Cancel Log stream Push events local flowgentic → asyncflow → rhapsody ConcurrentExecutionBackend (process pool) yes no no query httpx on the main event loop (REST retrieval) yes no no hpc (Orbit) EndpointRuntime with rhapsody and PSI/J plugins yes yes, by byte offset yes hpc (Globus) globus_compute_sdk.Executor only before start no no

Capabilities are declared rather than assumed, because the two HPC backends genuinely differ. A catalog of fourteen tasks (tasks/registry.py) says which interface each one belongs to and what it produces; TaskManager routes a submission to the right interface, and under logins it routes hpc work to the endpoint belonging to the user whose turn it is.

Three details make the remote path work and are not obvious from any single file:

  • A pool worker is handed its settings, not left to derive them. Task bodies call for settings themselves and cache the answer for the worker's lifetime, so changing anything a worker reads — the API key above all — requires a new pool, and therefore a rebuilt runtime.
  • Staging is in band. The broker forwards neither declared outputs nor stdin, so a spec that declares inputs or outputs is rewritten into a bash -lc script: inputs are gzipped, base64'd and split across argv, the real command's own chatter is pushed to stderr so stdout stays a clean data channel, and each output comes back as a framed block with its size and SHA-256. Framing is not optional — a login shell prints banners, and a stray > line is a valid FASTA header.
  • An HPC submission must carry a real job spec, or it degrades to /bin/true. The orchestrator fills the executable, executor, account and queue from settings, and the resource vocabulary is renamed into PSI/J's, which answers HTTP 500 on a field it does not recognize.

Where no HPC endpoint is attached, hpc tasks fall back to their app-local equivalents. The substitution is labelled at the point it happens — "no HPC endpoint was attached, so the job was never submitted" — because an unlabelled fallback makes a heuristic round indistinguishable from a real one. Where a real run does happen, its provenance is read rather than asserted: the model name and git hash are lifted out of ProteinMPNN's own FASTA header, and a run that declares neither earns a caveat saying so.

docs.title: The data lake, and what is shared
docs.text:
backend/designagent/lake/ is a three-tier design history behind a single DesignHistory facade.

Tier Store Holds 1 Kuzu, embedded graph raw outputs and provenance: Campaign, Reference, Design, Task, Output, Structure, joined by relations such as DERIVED_FROM and PRODUCED 2 SQLite scores, per-round rankings, analyses 3 Parquet plus a JSON manifest curated golden sets, staged for ML training behind explicit curation rules

Bulky payloads — coordinates, FASTA — go to a content-addressed blob directory and are referenced by path from tier 1. Tiers 1 and 2 are written together so they cannot drift. Every lake write is individually guarded: a storage failure must not lose a round the user waited two minutes for, so ranking falls back to in-memory and the user is told in the summary's caveats.

Two operational facts follow from Kuzu being an embedded database. It takes an exclusive file lock, so a second backend on the same data directory dies rather than degrading — and it sizes its buffer pool at roughly 80% of host RAM by default, which on a small VM is most of the machine, so there is an environment variable to cap it.

docs.title: Across sessions
docs.text: This is the point of the lake. A finished round is not just a message in a transcript: designs, tasks, outputs and scores are filed with their provenance, and a later session reads them back. DesignHistory.related_past_designs() returns the best designs on the current metric from other campaigns, and the interpreter surfaces them in the summary. The session summary artifact prints the tasks a round ran, with their interface and final state, straight out of the graph store — which is how you tell, weeks later, whether a design came off a cluster or out of a rule table.

docs.title: Across a group
docs.text:
With DESIGNAGENT_AUTH_ENABLED=true, one deployment serves several people. What is private to a user is their account, their chat sessions — a session that is not yours returns 404, because whether it exists is also the owner's business — and their credentials: eight fields covering an Anthropic key and model and an Orbit broker, token, certificate, endpoint, account and queue. Credentials are stored as Fernet ciphertext with each value cryptographically bound to its user and its field, so a ciphertext copied to another row fails to decrypt rather than silently becoming someone else's key. They are validated by rejection, and a broker must appear on an operator-configured allow-list, because it is a host the server will dial and hand a token to. A plain user's baseline has every operator credential removed, so nobody falls through to the operator's key or allocation, and every path, shell and scheduler choice stays operator-only.

What is shared, deliberately, is everything else: one design history, one checkpointer, one artifact store, for the whole deployment. Kuzu's exclusive lock rules out a data directory per user, and the cross-campaign read above is a feature for a lab working on related targets. The consequence must be stated plainly rather than discovered: on a shared deployment, one user's sessions can surface another user's designs.

Current tenancy limits

The Orbit broker is shared too, and every endpoint holds the broker token — so on a shared broker, any user can submit work as any other user. A deployment is therefore safe for one user, or for a group that trusts one another, and not for mutually untrusting tenants. One broker per user is specified in plans/LINODE_DEPLOY.md (Phase 3) and is not built. The remaining gaps left open by the current login implementation are recorded together in plans/BACKLOG.md (What Phase 2's logins leave open).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
A fresh public clone cannot be built yet

PEAT depends on four middleware packages — radical.asyncflow, rhapsody, flowgentic and radical.orbit — that are installed as local editable checkouts from a refcodes/ directory. That directory is gitignored and is not in the repository, so ./scripts/setup.sh on a clean clone stops and names what is missing rather than building a broken environment. You need those four checkouts separately; the revisions this project was last verified against are recorded in scripts/setup.sh. This is tracked in plans/BACKLOG.md as A fresh clone cannot be built, and it is the first thing to fix for outside users.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.12, via uv — setup.sh builds the virtual environment with uv venv --python 3.12. The package metadata allows 3.11 or newer.
  • Node.js with npm, for the frontend.
  • Local checkouts of the four middleware packages under refcodes/ (see the note above).
  • Optional: an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and an Orbit broker and endpoint for real HPC work. Neither is required to start the application.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/KhareLab/PEAT.git
cd PEAT
./scripts/setup.sh              # builds .venv and verifies it
cd frontend && npm install && cd ..

scripts/setup.sh is the only supported install path, and uv sync is not an alternative. flowgentic pins two of its own dependencies to git URLs that fight the local checkouts, so it is installed --no-deps; radical.orbit is installed the same way, with opentelemetry-sdk and nvidia-ml-py added by hand — without the OpenTelemetry SDK every rhapsody session inside Orbit fails to open, and the whole live test tier skips itself on an import error rather than failing. pyproject.toml carries the full reasoning where a [tool.uv.sources] block used to be.

Verify an existing environment without installing anything — run this after every pull, since it fails with the missing piece named rather than letting the application die deep inside an import:

./scripts/setup.sh --check

docs.title: Optional: a real ProteinMPNN
docs.text:
./scripts/setup_mpnn.sh          # ProteinMPNN (CPU) in .venv-mpnn
./scripts/setup_mpnn.sh --check  # verify, and print the variable to export

Deliberately not part of setup.sh: Torch is a ~200 MB download that no offline test needs. The script pins ProteinMPNN's revision, and --check prints the DESIGNAGENT_MPNN_COMMAND to export. With that plus the local Orbit stack, the hpc path runs the real model on your own host through a real broker — a 76-residue target takes a few seconds on CPU. That proves the model, not a scheduler, a queue or an allocation.

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
Settings come from environment variables with the prefix DESIGNAGENT_; .env.example lists them all with comments, and .env is resolved against the current working directory.

cp .env.example .env
.venv/bin/python -m designagent --check-config           # what is in effect, secrets masked
.venv/bin/python -m designagent --check-config --probe   # ...and whether each credential works

Precedence is: values set in the running application, then the environment, then .env, then the defaults in config.py. A credential is never rendered in full — responses carry presence, source and a masked hint — and nothing refuses to start: a missing or rejected credential shows up in /api/health, is badged in the UI, and makes the turn say in its reply that it fell back.

The settings that change behaviour most:

Variable Effect ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Enables LLM reasoning. Without it every node uses its rule-based path DESIGNAGENT_FOLD_BACKEND esmatlas (public API, ≤400 aa), local, or hpc DESIGNAGENT_MAX_ROUNDS Redesign rounds before the loop summarizes DESIGNAGENT_POOL_WORKERS Process-pool size DESIGNAGENT_ORBIT_ENABLED + RADICAL_ORBIT_* Remote HPC, with DESIGNAGENT_ORBIT_PSIJ_EXECUTOR, _ACCOUNT and _QUEUE for the site DESIGNAGENT_ORBIT_LOCAL Bring up a localhost broker and endpoint at startup, for development DESIGNAGENT_AUTH_ENABLED + DESIGNAGENT_SECRETS_KEY Per-user logins, and the Fernet key their credentials are stored under DESIGNAGENT_KUZU_BUFFER_POOL_MB Caps Kuzu's buffer pool; 0 keeps its default of ~80% of RAM, which on a small VM is most of the machine

A group of settings is environment-only and refused over HTTP — the data directory, the pool size, the ProteinMPNN command and prologue, and the whole DESIGNAGENT_PROTOCOL_* group. Each names a path or a shell word the server will run, locally or on the endpoint under the site's allocation, so accepting them over a settings route would make that route arbitrary code execution. They are reported read-only in the UI so you can see the value without being offered an edit that would fail.

Run everything from the repository root

config.yml is read from the current working directory at import flowgentic time, and both its agent_execution and logger keys must be present.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./scripts/dev.sh up           # backend on :8000, frontend on :5173, endpoint if installed
./scripts/dev.sh up --no-mpnn # no endpoint: the heuristic path
./scripts/dev.sh down | status | restart | logs

Or start the two halves by hand — .venv/bin/python -m designagent --reload and, in another shell, cd frontend && npm run dev. dev.sh does the same thing and also handles four traps worth knowing about either way: Kuzu's exclusive lock means a second backend on the same data directory dies rather than degrading, so up refuses and names the holder; the backend does not stop on SIGTERM, because the workflow engine installs its own handler, reports a completed shutdown and leaves the process running, so every stop has to escalate; the local Orbit endpoint registers a few seconds after the port opens, so up waits for the health endpoint to report hpc: true — a round planned before then silently takes the heuristic branch; and a naive pgrep for the server's command line matches the shell running it and kills itself.

Then open http://localhost:5173 and ask for something, for example "redesign 1UBQ to improve thermostability".

docs.title: Against a real HPC endpoint
docs.text:
DESIGNAGENT_ORBIT_ENABLED=true \
RADICAL_ORBIT_BROKER_URL=https://<broker-host>:<port> \
RADICAL_ORBIT_BROKER_CERT=/path/to/broker_cert.pem \
RADICAL_ORBIT_BROKER_TOKEN=<token> \
DESIGNAGENT_ORBIT_PSIJ_EXECUTOR=slurm \
DESIGNAGENT_ORBIT_ACCOUNT=<account> \
.venv/bin/python -m designagent

Standing the broker and the endpoint up is its own exercise; plans/AMAREL_ENDPOINT.md in the repository is the runbook, with an acceptance ladder whose rungs record what they actually returned. For development, DESIGNAGENT_ORBIT_LOCAL=true has the server bring up a localhost broker plus an endpoint itself, so the real client path is exercised with no allocation.

docs.title: Turning logins on
docs.text:
Logins are off unless DESIGNAGENT_AUTH_ENABLED=true, and off they change nothing: one implicit user, and every ownership check passes. On, every route but login, logout and a bare health check needs the session cookie, a chat session must belong to the caller, and the operator's settings routes need an admin role.

Accounts are made from the CLI, in the server's own environment, never over HTTP:

.venv/bin/python -m designagent --gen-secrets-key          # a DESIGNAGENT_SECRETS_KEY
.venv/bin/python -m designagent --add-user NAME [--admin]  # an account
.venv/bin/python -m designagent --passwd NAME              # set a password
.venv/bin/python -m designagent --list-users

Each signed-in user then supplies their own Anthropic key and their own Orbit broker, token, certificate, endpoint, account and queue, which replace the operator's for their turns only. Read what a multi-user deployment shares before inviting a second person: the design history and the broker are both shared.

Behind a reverse proxy

Behind a same-host proxy every caller looks like loopback, so the settings routes that are deliberately open on loopback are open to the internet unless logins or an admin token close them. Keep the secrets key in the same backup as the broker's key — losing it makes every user re-enter their credentials.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q            # 417 tests, offline; stubs replace every tool
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q -m live    # 12 tests; starts a real Orbit broker + endpoint
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q -m remote  # 8 tests; submits to a real HPC endpoint
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q -m llm     # 4 tests; calls Anthropic with a real key

cd frontend && npm test                      # 45 tests in jsdom; no servers needed
cd frontend && npm run test:e2e              # 2 tests in Chromium, canned stream
cd frontend && E2E_LIVE=1 npm run test:e2e   # ...plus one real round trip
.venv/bin/ruff check backend tests           # E/F/I, line length 100

The offline tier needs no network, no process pool and no endpoint, because nodes reach the outside only through injected dependencies. The other three tiers are each deselected separately in pyproject.toml, so that -m live cannot drag in a tier that needs an allocation or spends money — and a marker is the only thing that selects them, so naming the file alone collects nothing. Chromium needs a one-time npx playwright install chromium.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: The stack is in four parts: the Python packages the server declares, four middleware packages it deliberately does not declare, the frontend's own small set, and the external services the agent calls at runtime.

docs.title: Python runtime dependencies
docs.text:
Declared in pyproject.toml, grouped as that file groups them. The package requires Python 3.11 or newer, and scripts/setup.sh builds the environment with 3.12.

Group Packages Agent loop langgraph>=1.2,<2, langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite, langchain-core>=1.6,<2, langchain>=1.4,<2, langchain-anthropic, python-json-logger, pyyaml, python-dotenv Web fastapi, uvicorn[standard], httpx, pydantic>=2, pydantic-settings Data lake and artifacts kuzu, pyarrow, python-docx, biopython

Three further dependencies are there only to satisfy upstream code, and are commented as such at their declaration:

  • langchain-openai and langchain-ollama are not used by this project. import flowgentic pulls in a provider module that imports both at module scope, so they must be installed.
  • aiohttp is required because flowgentic's retry machinery wraps its optional httpx and aiohttp imports in try: ... except Exception: raise, which makes both hard requirements.

Optional groups:

uv pip install -e '.[dev]'    # pytest, pytest-asyncio, respx, ruff
uv pip install -e '.[chem]'   # ChemGraph: cheminformatics / quantum chemistry

ChemGraph is heavy and pins langgraph, langchain and pydantic exactly while pulling Torch through mace-torch, so install it deliberately and re-check the resolved set afterwards.

docs.title: The four middleware packages
docs.text:
Package Role radical.asyncflow The workflow engine tasks are submitted through rhapsody Execution backends, including the ConcurrentExecutionBackend process pool the local interface uses flowgentic The LangGraph ↔ asyncflow integration: tasks are wrapped as flowgentic function tasks radical.orbit The broker, the endpoint runtime, and the rhapsody and PSI/J plugins behind the hpc interface

They are deliberately absent from pyproject.toml, and there is no [tool.uv.sources] block. All four are local editable installs from a refcodes/ directory, applied by scripts/setup.sh.

The reason is recorded in pyproject.toml itself. Declaring them makes uv sync the obvious command, and it cannot work: flowgentic pins radical-asyncflow and academy-py to git URLs, so resolving its dependencies fetches from git and fights the local checkout. It is therefore installed --no-deps, and the three packages it then lacks (academy, langchain-community, langchain-mcp-adapters) are on no path this project uses. A previous [tool.uv.sources] block listed three of them while none was a declared dependency, so uv sync resolved cleanly and silently produced an environment that died at import flowgentic.

radical.orbit is installed --no-deps for a related reason — its requirements name the published rhapsody-py, which would displace the editable checkout — with its real needs installed by name alongside, including psij-python, globus-sdk, msgpack, cloudpickle, websockets and authlib. Two more are added by hand: opentelemetry-sdk, without which every rhapsody session inside Orbit fails to open, and nvidia-ml-py.

Because refcodes/ is gitignored, the revisions this project was last built and checked against are recorded in scripts/setup.sh as REFCODES_PINS, and --check warns on a mismatch rather than failing — a newer checkout may well be fine, but the repository's claims about these packages were made against those commits.

docs.title: Known rough edges, worked around at the call site
docs.text:
1. flowgentic's examples import ConcurrentExecutionBackend from radical.asyncflow, where it no longer exists; it lives in rhapsody.backends.
  2. _default_retryable_exceptions() re-raises on a failed optional import, making httpx and aiohttp hard requirements. Both are installed, and retryable exceptions are passed explicitly.
  3. flowgentic's default retry configuration is a 30-second timeout with three attempts, which would cancel and silently re-run a fold or an HPC job. Tasks are wrapped with no timeout and a single attempt.
  4. Orbit's clients are synchronous and its push callbacks arrive on a listener thread, so calls are run in a thread and events are hopped back onto the event loop. Its terminal task event omits stdout, so the result is re-fetched.

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text:
frontend/package.json declares four runtime dependencies:

Package Version Role react / react-dom ^19.0.0 The UI marked ^15.0.6 Renders assistant Markdown dompurify ^3.2.3 Sanitizes it, because assistant text is model-influenced

The build and test set is vite ^6, typescript ~5.7, @vitejs/plugin-react, vitest with jsdom and Testing Library for the unit tier, and @playwright/test for the Chromium tier.

The Mol* viewer is not an npm dependency. frontend/src/artifacts/MolstarView.tsx loads @rcsb/rcsb-molstar (pinned to a specific version in that file) as a UMD bundle from jsDelivr at runtime and caches the loader on window. The structure viewer therefore needs network access from the browser, not from the server.
